sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: X \sim \textrm{Multinomial}(10, \mathbf{p})] where [MATH: \mathbf{p}=(p_1,0.1,0.2,0.5),] find [MATH: P(X_2=1,X_3=2,X_4=3).] Round your answer to [MATH: 3] decimal places.
sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: X \sim \textrm{Multinomial}(10, \mathbf{p})] where [MATH: \mathbf{p}=(p_1,0.1,0.2,0.5),] find [MATH: P(X_2=1,X_3=2,X_4=3).] Round your answer to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that the multinomial probability mass function of [MATH: X\sim \textrm{Multinomial}(n, \mathbf{p})] is given by

[MATH: f(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_k)=\dfrac{n!}{x_1!\,x_2!\, \cdots \,x_k!} \, p_1^{x_1}p_2^{x_2}\cdots p_k^{x_k},]

where [MATH: x_i] are nonnegative integers such that [MATH: \displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^k x_i = n] and [MATH: \displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^k p_i = 1.]

As a result, we can solve for [MATH: p_1{:}]

[MATH: p_{1} + p_{2} + p_{3} + p_{4}|= 1; p_{1} + 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.5|= 1; p_{1}|= 0.2]

We can also solve for [MATH: x_1{:}]

[MATH: x_{1} + x_{2} + x_{3} + x_{4}|= n; x_{1} + 1 + 2 + 3|= 10; x_{1}|= 4]

So, we have

[MATH: n = 10, p = (0.2, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5), x_{1} = 4, x_{2} = 1, x_{3} = 2, x_{4} = 3.]

Therefore, for our multinomial random variable [MATH: X,] we obtain

[MATH: P(X_{2} = 1, X_{3} = 2, X_{4} = 3)|= P(X_{1} = 4, X_{2} = 1, X_{3} = 2, X_{4} = 3); = f(4, 1, 2, 3); = (10!)/(4!1!2!3!)(0.2)^{4}(0.1)^{1}(0.2)^{2}(0.5)^{3}; ≈ 0.010]

rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: X_1,] [MATH: X_2, X_3,] and [MATH: X_4] be the number of customers that buy chocolate, strawberry, vanilla, or another flavor of ice cream, respectively. Then, the corresponding probabilities are

[MATH: p_1=0.3, \qquad p_2=0.2, \qquad p_3=0.1, \qquad p_4=0.4.]

This situation can be modeled using a multinomial distribution.

Recall that the multinomial probability mass function of [MATH: X\sim \textrm{Multinomial}(n, \mathbf{p})] is given by

[MATH: f(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_k)=\dfrac{n!}{x_1!\,x_2!\, \cdots \,x_k!} \, p_1^{x_1}p_2^{x_2}\cdots p_k^{x_k},]

where [MATH: x_i] are nonnegative integers such that [MATH: \displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^k x_i = n] and [MATH: \displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^k p_i = 1.]

In our case, we have

[MATH: n = 7, p = (0.3, 0.2, 0.1, 0.4)x_{1} = 2, x_{2} = 1, x_{3} = 2]

and

[MATH: x_{4}|= n − x_{1} − x_{2} − x_{3}; = 7 − 2 − 1 − 2; = 2.]

Therefore, for our multinomial distribution [MATH: X,] we obtain

[MATH: P(X_{1} = 2, X_{2} = 1, X_{3} = 2, X_{4} = 2)|= (7!)/(2!1!2!2!)(0.3)^{2}(0.2)^{1}(0.1)^{2}(0.4)^{2}; ≈ 0.018.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider a trial that results in exactly one of some fixed finite number [MATH: k] of mutually exclusive outcomes with probabilities [MATH: p_1], [MATH: p_
2, \ldots, p_k] such that
[MATH: p_1+p_2+\ldots+p_k=1]
and there are [MATH: n] independent trials.

Content:
Let the random variables [MATH: X_i] indicate the number of times outcome [MATH: i] was observed over the [MATH: n] trials. Then, the tuple
[MATH: X = (X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_k)]
follows a multinomial distribution with parameters [MATH: n] and [MATH: p=(p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_k)], and we write
[MATH: X \sim \textrm{Multinomial}(n, p).]

Content:
For example, suppose we throw a fair tetrahedral die [MATH: 10] times. Let the random variables [MATH: X_i] for [MATH: i = 1, 2,3,4] denote the number of times [MATH: i] is observed. Then, the random tuple

Content:
[MATH: X = (X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4)]
follows a multinomial distribution. We have [MATH: p_i=\dfrac{1}{4}] for all [MATH: i,] and

Content:
[MATH: X \sim \textrm{Multinomial}\left(10, \left(\dfrac 14,\dfrac 14, \dfrac 14, \dfrac 14\right)\right).]

Content:
The multinomial probability mass function of [MATH: X=(X_1,\ldots, X_k) \sim \textrm{Multinomial}(n, p)] is given by

Content:
[MATH: f(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_k)=P(X_1=x_1,X_2=x_2,\ldots,X_{k}=x_{k})=\dfrac{n!}{x_1!\,x_2!\,\cdots\, x_k!}p_1^{x_1}p_2^{x_2}\cdot\ldots\cdot p_k^{x_k},]

Content:
where the [MATH: x_i]'s are nonnegative integers that sum to [MATH: n.]

Content:
Finally, note that the marginal distribution of each [MATH: X_i] is

Content:
[MATH: X_i\sim B(n,p_j).]

---

Item 2 — Example: Computing a Probability at a Point

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: X \sim \textrm{Multinomial}(10, \mathbf{p})] where [MATH: \mathbf{p}=(p_1,0.1,0.2,0.5),] find [MATH: P(X_2=1,X_3=2,X_4=3).] Round your answer to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that the multinomial probability mass function of [MATH: X\sim \textrm{Multinomial}(n, \mathbf{p})] is given by

[MATH: f(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_k)=\dfrac{n!}{x_1!\,x_2!\, \cdots \,x_k!} \, p_1^{x_1}p_2^{x_2}\cdots p_k^{x_k},]

where [MATH: x_i] are nonnegative integers such that [MATH: \displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^k x_i = n] and [MATH: \displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^k p_i = 1.]

As a result, we can solve for [MATH: p_1{:}]

[MATH: p_{1} + p_{2} + p_{3} + p_{4}|= 1; p_{1} + 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.5|= 1; p_{1}|= 0.2]

We can also solve for [MATH: x_1{:}]

[MATH: x_{1} + x_{2} + x_{3} + x_{4}|= n; x_{1} + 1 + 2 + 3|= 10; x_{1}|= 4]

So, we have

[MATH: n = 10, p = (0.2, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5), x_{1} = 4, x_{2} = 1, x_{3} = 2, x_{4} = 3.]

Therefore, for our multinomial random variable [MATH: X,] we obtain

[MATH: P(X_{2} = 1, X_{3} = 2, X_{4} = 3)|= P(X_{1} = 4, X_{2} = 1, X_{3} = 2, X_{4} = 3); = f(4, 1, 2, 3); = (10!)/(4!1!2!3!)(0.2)^{4}(0.1)^{1}(0.2)^{2}(0.5)^{3}; ≈ 0.010]

rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

In our case, we have
[MATH: n = 7, p = (0.1, 0.2, 0.2, 0.5)]
and
[MATH: x_{4}|= n − x_{1} − x_{2} − x_{3}; = 7 − x_{1} − x_{2} − x_{3}.]

Therefore, for our multinomial random variable [MATH: X,] we obtain
[MATH: P(X_{1} = 1, 1 < X_{2} ≤ 3, X_{3} = 2)|= P(X_{1} = 1, X_{2} ∈ {2, 3}, X_{3} = 2); = P(X_{1} = 1, X_{2} = 2, X_{3} = 2); = + P(X_{1} = 1, X_{2} = 3, X_{3} = 2); = P(X_{1} = 1, X_{2} = 2, X_{3} = 2, X_{4} = 2); = + P(X_{1} = 1, X_{2} = 3, X_{3} = 2, X_{4} = 1); = (7!)/(1!2!2!2!)(0.1)^{1}(0.2)^{2}(0.2)^{2}(0.5)^{2}; = + (7!)/(1!3!2!1!)(0.1)^{1}(0.2)^{3}(0.2)^{2}(0.5)^{1}; ≈ 0.032]
